newsitem.title: FRANCE: Louvre museum gives fashion relics permanent home.
newsitem.headline: Louvre museum gives fashion relics permanent home.

text.p: A new fashion museum is opening on Saturday in a wing of the Louvre and its three floors will be crammed with such treasures as the wooden hoops of an 18th century gown, Coco Chanel's gold-beaded flapper dress and Paco Rabanne's 1969 metal-disc mini.
Gowns, girdles and jewel-embroidered pumps will be on display in the Paris museum's new Musee de la Mode, which will take up three newly refurbished floors of the museum's Rohan Wing.

The exhibits represent just one percent of the 81,000-piece collection which is among the three largest fashion collections in the world. The other two are London's Victoria and Albert Museum and the Metropolitan Museum of Art in New York.
Twice a year, the permanent exhibit will be rotated so that eventually all 16,000 outfits, 35,000 accessories and 30,000 fabric and embroidery samples will be on public display.
The opening coincides with the conclusion of this year's spring-summer haute couture collections.

Co-sponsored by Balmain, Hermes, Elle magazine and luxury giant LVMH -- which owns Dior, Christian Lacroix and Givenchy -- the exhibit offers a thoroughly documented trip down memory lane as part of Paris' efforts to reinforce its role as the world's fashion capital.

Arranged in reverse chronological order from the 1990s back to the French revolution, the exhibit offers such artifacts as a 1967 Pucci cape of psychedelic scarf silk, an orange vinyl maxi by Andre Courrege and a pair of snakeskin platform shoes, circa 1972.

One of its historical gems is Christian Dior's famous 1947 ivory shantung jacket and petticoated black skirt that introduced the revolutionary "New Look", stirring up a fury with its cinched waist, sloping shoulders and generous skirting that would stamp out memories of the privations of World War Two and govern style for the next decade.
A black and white checkerboard velveteen sheath by Jeanne Lanvin, and Elsa Schiaparelli's satin column of fuschia and black bands are examples of the 1930's streamlined elegance.

A statuesque black gown strewn with sculpted velvet flowers is the sole relic of haute couture's founder, Englishman Charles Frederick Worth, who opened his Paris salon in 1858 and became the dressmaker of Empress Eugenie and Princess Metternich.

Other treasures include the rich tasselled and trimmed "visites" -- short cape-like jackets of 1880s high society -- the dainty roses stitched on a boned Directoire corset and a Nehru suit by Thierry Mugler.
Flamboyant former culture minister Jack Lang stirred outrage in 1985 when he wore the suit to the French parliament without a tie.
Almost all of the pieces are private donations, including 150 dresses from designer Madeleine Vionnet's personal collection which she created between 1919 and 1939.
Spaniard Cristobal Balenciaga gave 74 pieces while Denise Boulet-Poiret, the wife of couturier Paul Poiret, contributed 32 of her husband's outfits.
